LINE, in its original formulation, does not use a Generative Adversarial Network or a Wasserstein discriminator minimax game to optimize its first-order and second-order proximity objectives. Instead, LINE learns node embeddings by maximizing the likelihood of observed edges under two separate objectives: first-order proximity (for directly connected node pairs) and second-order proximity (for preserving neighborhood distributions). In the standard LINE training procedure, the model parameters are updated with stochastic gradient descent, typically using negative sampling to approximate the softmax normalization.

Under the user’s hypothetical GAN-Wasserstein reinterpretation, a reasonable mapping is as follows. The generator would produce or adjust edge weights so that sampled edges from the reconstructed network better match the original network’s edge distribution. The discriminator would score real versus generated edges, and its gradients would push the generator to increase weights on edges that improve the match to observed connectivity patterns while decreasing weights on implausible edges. For first-order proximity, this would mean strengthening weights on observed edges between adjacent nodes; for second-order proximity, it would mean adjusting weights so that nodes with similar neighborhoods receive higher compatibility scores even if they are not directly connected.

However, this is only a speculative extension. In the actual LINE algorithm, there is no explicit generator network, no discriminator network, and no direct adversarial update rule for edge weights. LINE instead optimizes embedding vectors and, in the second-order case, context vectors; edge weights are not learned as a separate adversarial parameterization. If one wanted to implement the hypothetical GAN version, the generator would likely parameterize edge probabilities or weights in the reconstructed network, while the discriminator would estimate Wasserstein distance between real and generated edge samples, and both would be updated alternately by gradient-based optimization.
